scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

My mom has been hosting Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve for about 50 years, and now she's too old, so we, her four kids, are supposed to take over, rotating each year. So far, each of us has hosted one holiday. This year, it's my turn to host Thanksgiving. But here's the thing: my wife's family is planning to go to the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. They invited all their kids and grandkids, and my wife really wants to go. Our daughter also wants to go because it's a once-in-a-lifetime event. I want to go too. So, we decided to go, and then I called my older brother to figure out what to do about Thanksgiving since I can't host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be mad and that I should tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I called her, and she was mad. She said she'll probably have to end up hosting even though it's her turn for Christmas. She accused me of being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. She also mentioned that Mom would be sad if I abandon Thanksgiving to go to New York. I offered to pay for them to rent a place and have it catered, but she said that takes away from the close-knit family vibe. My brother mentioned his wife might be up for hosting, but he didn't sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can't host because she's renovating her house. I feel bad about backing out of my turn, but I tried to offer solutions. I also offered to host the next holiday, but my oldest sister said no because it's her turn and she's been planning it all year. Next up is my brother, so I suggested swapping Thanksgiving if his wife is up for it. Now, the question is: Am I in the wrong here? Let me break this down. The family tradition is important, and my mom has been hosting for decades. We agreed to rotate hosting, so each of us is supposed to take turns. This year was my turn, but I decided to go to the parade with my wife's family instead. That means I can't host, which affects the family plan. On one hand, family traditions and honoring my mom's wishes are significant. She's been the backbone of these gatherings, and we agreed to take over. By not hosting, I'm breaking that agreement. My sister is upset because she now has to host, which was supposed to be her turn for Christmas. That's a burden on her, especially since she's already planning for Christmas. On the other hand, my wife's family event is a big deal, and it's a rare opportunity for us to spend time with her relatives. Our daughter is excited too. It's a special event, and it's understandable that I want to prioritize that. I tried to offer solutions, like paying for a venue and catering, but my sister didn't like that idea because it changes the family vibe. I also offered to host the next holiday, but she refused. My brother might be able to host, but he's not enthusiastic about it. So, am I in the wrong? I think I need to consider the importance of family traditions, the commitments we made, and the feelings of my siblings. It's a tough spot because I want to honor my mom's wishes and keep the tradition alive, but I also have other family obligations and opportunities. Maybe I should have communicated earlier or tried harder to find a solution that works for everyone. But I did try to offer help, so I'm not entirely in the wrong. However, by choosing to go to the parade, I did break the family agreement, which might make me partially responsible for the disruption.
